It uses HBM, not GDDR, on an interposer. One of the most important things about it is that it uses significantly less power than GDDR, which means you can then clock the GPU more aggressively as GPUs only have roughly a 275w power limit (though some go beyond specifications and go beyond that). IIRC, GDDR can take up to 50w of power, leaving the other 275w to 300w for the GPU and other parts of the graphics card. HBM uses a fraction of that, IIRC it's like 10w or 20w. Which means you can increase GPU performance to use that additional power. Not to mention it makes a lot of bandwidth compared to GDDR5, and the latency is a lot better too, which is important for VR. It's superior to GDDR5 (and GDDR5x) in nearly every way, except price. The new Nvidia cards will be having it when they come out (rumors are now that GP100 will show up in Q1 2017, and it'll probably not make it into GP104 (GTX 1070, 1080)). AMD just has a huge head start on Nvidia with regards to memory technology.
